title: Storm Adam aid, rental proposals and property tax rulings
summary:
Storm Adam has killed six people, and Valencia has approved aid for affected households. We cover proposed rental changes, property tax rulings, pay developments and the election campaign, plus pension access and a savings offer.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For households whose homes flooded, the help now includes—

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: —housing aid. Valencia approved support yesterday after Storm Adam killed six people across Spain.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Families need somewhere to live while they deal with the damage.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: They do. Rehousing support is part of the package.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good morning. It's Wednesday, the twenty-first of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'm Inna, here with Dima. Today: proposed rental changes and property tax inspections. First, Storm Adam and Valencia's aid.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Storm Adam has killed six people across Spain since October seventeenth, El Mundo reports. Valencia's government approved aid yesterday for affected coastal areas in southern Valencia and northern Alicante. Urgent payments include six thousand euros for damaged main homes, with support for second homes too.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Families who lost their main home can receive monthly rehousing support. A single application can be submitted through the regional government's portal, town halls or local public-service offices. Free legal, notarial and registry assistance will help with insurance procedures and claims.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Inna, having those application routes matters when people are dealing with damage and insurance at the same time.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It does. People can apply in person rather than relying entirely on an online process.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: But housing isn't the whole loss. What about cars and businesses?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: A further package is planned in the coming days for those losses, including farming, hospitality and animal shelters.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Town halls get money too, for urgent costs. So the help isn't only going to individual families.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For rental households, Heraldo reports a proposed change awaiting a parliamentary vote that's unlikely to pass. Landlords declining renewal would owe at least twelve months' rent for a similar home. After the minimum term, contracts would renew for five years unless valid notice is given.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Hold on. Would landlords need to watch the expiry date more closely, Inna?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: If this passes, yes. Missing valid notice could mean a much longer renewal, rather than another annual extension. mhm

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And tenants would have more stability. Though planning a move around a pending vote isn't easy.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Staying with housing, the government has approved a hundred and eighty million euros for regions applying the housing law's rent caps. El Diario says that's double September's announcement. The money can support affordable housing and cover unpaid rent.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Oh, a bigger pot. Can you use it for homes that already exist, not just new building?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Regions can buy existing homes for affordable or social rent, so construction isn't the only route. I see

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Europa Press reports that the Supreme Court has granted amnesty to former Catalan vice-president Oriol Junqueras. Former Catalan ministers Raül Romeva, Jordi Turull and Dolors Bassa also received amnesty. The ruling follows the Constitutional Court's endorsement of amnesty for embezzlement, the crime for which they were convicted.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: How long has the amnesty law been in force, Dima?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Two years. And with the election on the twenty-ninth of November, the ruling carries real political weight.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Another Supreme Court ruling concerns property tax valuations. El Confidencial reports that Tax Agency experts must inspect both the interior and exterior. The cadastre, Spain's property map, Google Maps and aerial photographs alone aren't enough. Taxpayers can challenge reassessments made without a physical inspection, for example for inheritance or property transfer taxes.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Wait, the expert has to come inside? Looking at the roof on a screen won't do.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The condition inside matters too. If your valuation was done remotely, this ruling gives you grounds to challenge it. mhm

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For homebuyers in Madrid, Expansión reports another tax ruling. Families expecting a third child can qualify for the four percent transfer-tax rate instead of six percent. The child must have been conceived when the main-home purchase was signed and must be born alive. The large-family certificate needn't exist at signing.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Ah, the certificate doesn't have to arrive before the house keys. Can families who've already paid seek money back?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Families who paid the general rate in similar circumstances may request refunds. That could make a substantial difference. oh good

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: There's another family tax decision, this time about personal income tax. El País reports that the Supreme Court allows parents with shared custody to deduct child maintenance payments. The ruling corrects the Tax Agency's position and rejects penalising parents for both caring for their children and paying maintenance.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Huh. So paying maintenance and sharing the care at the same time shouldn't cost you extra in tax.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For separated parents who share custody and pay maintenance, the ruling may reduce their income tax bill.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: On household budgets, El País reports that inflation is outpacing average negotiated wage adjustments. Collective bargaining has stalled, and six in ten sectoral or company pay agreements lack automatic inflation revision clauses. That leaves many workers losing buying power as prices rise faster than their pay.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oof. A pay rise can look welcome on paper and still leave the shopping budget tighter. true

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Exactly. Without that automatic adjustment, the agreement itself doesn't catch wages up when prices climb.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For public employees, Europa Press reports a government guarantee of a four-point-five percent rise from January first next year. The existing agreement covers more than three million employees. Unions want formal approval before the November twenty-ninth election. An additional inflation-linked payment for this year remains conditional.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Okay, there's a date employees can plan around. Are the unions asking for the paperwork before election day?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: They are. The rise is already in the agreement, but they want it formally approved before the vote.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: In the campaign, Veinte Minutos reports that the People's Party and Vox may be exploring a Senate alliance. The Socialists and Frente Amplio have registered a coalition seeking to end the People's Party's absolute majority. The Senate helps select Constitutional Court members and other key officeholders through appointments requiring reinforced majorities.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Really, the upper house is drawing this much attention? Those appointments explain why the alliances matter beyond election night.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: They do. Control there affects who can make or block appointments to the courts, the public broadcaster and the Ombudsman.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For some citizens abroad, voting eligibility is being checked. Europa Press says forty-eight consular offices have wholly or partly verified citizens naturalised under the grandchildren's law. Under a Supreme Court ruling, only those verified as descendants of exiles can vote in the November twenty-ninth election.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: How many people are we talking about?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: More than a hundred and sixty thousand people in the voter census, according to the report. And a Constitutional Court decision is still pending.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: On the street, El País reports that protests and a possible general strike are dividing parties. The government believes left-wing mobilisation could help it. Opponents criticise the protests and draw comparisons with France, with housing demonstrations and education strikes entering the campaign debate.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Is there a date for that possible general strike?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The eleventh of November comes up in the debate. So it lands right in the middle of the campaign.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For bereaved unmarried partners, Europa Press reports a widow's pension measure approved by the cabinet yesterday. It offers a one-year claim window for past deaths where the couple had children and lived together for more than two years. They must have been neither married nor registered partners, and previously claimed the pension. Parliamentary validation is required.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Does that include someone whose earlier pension claim was denied?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It may, if they meet those conditions and Parliament validates the decree.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And a savings offer to finish. Expansión reports that Arquia Banca's one-year welcome deposit pays three percent annually. Applications close October thirtieth, and the money must come from another bank. Interest is paid at maturity. Partial withdrawals aren't allowed, and closing early means losing all interest.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oh, there's the catch. You need to be comfortable leaving the money untouched.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Right. Close early and you get your deposit back, but none of the return.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The immediate priority is help for storm-hit households, alongside decisions affecting housing costs, taxes and pay.
